data.name: Reactive oxygen species
data.description: ROS generated by mitochondrial activity, both a consequence and a driver of mTOR signalling.

reading_levels.student: ROS generated by mitochondrial activity, both a consequence and a driver of mTOR signalling.
reading_levels.research: Bidirectional and therefore a loop, not an arrow: unleashing mTORC1 by deleting TSC1 floods haematopoietic stem cells with ROS and exhausts them, rescued by an antioxidant (CHE2008); conversely oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K–Akt–mTORC1–eIF4A cascade (JIN2026). Which direction dominates depends on cell type and how sustained the oxidative load is.

studies.title: Redox-sensitive mTOR-eIF4A signaling promotes selective P-glycoprotein translation.
studies.authors: Jin P; Jin M; Feng L; He J; Yin Y; Bai R; Feng T; Zhang T; Luo H; Ma X; Chen J; Hussain S; Wan S; Fang Z; Wu Y; Luo L

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A cascade that selectively promotes P-glycoprotein translation via cap-dependent mRNA engagement, revealing a transcription-independent mechanism of rapid multidrug resistance induction.

studies.title: TSC-mTOR maintains quiescence and function of hematopoietic stem cells by repressing mitochondrial biogenesis and reactive oxygen species
studies.authors: Chen C; Liu Yu; Liu R; Ikenoue T; Guan KL; Liu Yang; Zheng P

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Showed why blood stem cells must keep mTOR LOW. Deleting TSC1 (which unleashes mTOR) drove resting stem cells into rapid division, flooded them with reactive oxygen species, and burned out their ability to self-renew. An antioxidant rescued them. A key link between mTOR, stem-cell exhaustion, and tissue aging.

studies.title: Redox activation of ATG5 licenses autophagy upon nutrient restriction
studies.authors: Shin S; Korobkina ED; Lennicke C; Burger N; Zhang B; Xiao H; Wang Y; Petrocelli JJ; Wei SM; Wood D; Lei Y; Zhang X; Perez-Matos MC; Sharif MA; Zhang J; Cochemé HM; Mair WB; Chouchani ET

evidence.label: Preprint, not peer-reviewed
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human cell lines and mice; tissue-resolved cysteine redox proteomics (OxiDR atlas) under dietary restriction
studies.finding: Dietary restriction selectively oxidizes a specific, tissue-resolved set of cysteines rather than oxidizing the proteome broadly. One of the most strongly oxidized is Cys19 on the core autophagy protein ATG5; this oxidation is required for ATG5 to bind ATG10 and form the ATG5-ATG12 conjugate that lipidates LC3B and builds the autophagosome. In mice lacking this redox switch, nutrient restriction fails to trigger autophagy, causing severe tissue pathology and early death -- a single oxidized cysteine gates the autophagic response to fasting.

studies.title: ATM signals to TSC2 in the cytoplasm to regulate mTORC1 in response to ROS
studies.authors: Alexander A; Cai SL; Kim J; Nanez A; Sahin M; MacLean KH; Inoki K; Guan KL; Shen J; Person MD; Kusewitt D; Mills GB; Kastan MB; Walker CL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Cell lines with ATM loss or ROS exposure; Atm-deficient mice treated with rapamycin
studies.finding: Described a cytoplasmic job for the DNA-damage kinase ATM. In response to raised ROS, ATM activated TSC2 through LKB1 and AMPK, which repressed mTORC1 and induced autophagy. ATM-deficient cells had high ROS and poorly controlled mTORC1, and rapamycin lowered both and delayed lymphoma formation in Atm-deficient mice. Boundary: worked from the abstract only (PMC record without retrievable text); cell lines and mice. Note that the Atlas edge ROS-MTORC1 describes the opposite sign in another context, so the effect of ROS on mTORC1 depends on source and setting.

relations.mechanism: Unleashing mTORC1 by deleting TSC1 drives quiescent haematopoietic stem cells into cycle, raises mitochondrial biogenesis and floods them with ROS; an antioxidant rescues self-renewal.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Switching mTORC1 on too much pushes resting stem cells to start dividing and floods them with reactive, damaging molecules; giving them antioxidants restores their normal function.
relations.boundary: Demonstrated in haematopoietic stem cells, where quiescence is the baseline state. Cell types that are already cycling need not behave this way.

relations.mechanism: Oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K–Akt–mTORC1–eIF4A cascade that selectively promotes cap-dependent translation of P-glycoprotein.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Oxidative damage can itself switch on mTORC1 through a chain of signals, closing a feedback loop that can turn a brief stress into a lasting one.
relations.boundary: One cell-line study in a multidrug-resistance context; whether the loop runs in normal physiology at these ROS levels is untested.
